issue.issue_text: Whether a complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act should be quashed on the ground that the accused had resigned from the partnership firm before the cheque was issued.

facts: A criminal complaint was filed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments (NI) Act against a partnership firm and its partners, including the appellant.
The appellant sought to have the complaint against him quashed on two main grounds.
The specific ground in question was that he had resigned from the partnership firm on May 28, 2013, which was more than two years before the cheque in question was issued on August 21, 2015.
law: Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments (NI) Act, 1881, pertains to the offense of a dishonored cheque.
Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.PC) grants the High Court the inherent power to quash criminal proceedings to prevent an abuse of the process of the court.
application: The High Court, whose decision was being appealed, considered the appellant's argument about his resignation.
The High Court determined that the claim of having resigned from the partnership firm prior to the issuance of the cheque is a factual contention.
It reasoned that such a fact needs to be proven by the appellant by leading evidence during a trial.

Consequently, the High Court held that this factual dispute could not be decided at the initial stage in a proceeding under Section 482 Cr.PC, which is meant for quashing complaints based on legal or procedural defects apparent on the face of the record, not for conducting a mini-trial on disputed facts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court noted the High Court's decision, which rejected the argument to quash the complaint based on the appellant's resignation. The High Court concluded that the resignation was a 'matter of evidence' that the appellant would have to prove during the trial, and therefore, it was not a valid ground for quashing the complaint at the preliminary stage.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complaint is liable to be quashed for being devoid of the mandatory averments required under Section 141(1) of the NI Act to fasten vicarious liability on the appellant.

facts: A criminal complaint was filed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments (NI) Act against a partnership firm and its partners, including the appellant.
The appellant sought to quash the complaint, arguing that it lacked the specific allegations required under Section 141(1) of the NI Act to hold him vicariously liable.
The complaint alleged that the partners were "responsible for the day-to-day contact and business" of the firm and that the firm, through its partners, had approached the complainant.
law: Section 141(1) of the NI Act establishes vicarious liability for officers of a company or partners of a firm for an offence committed by the entity.

To hold a person vicariously liable, the complaint must specifically allege that at the time the offence was committed, the person was "in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company."
The Supreme Court clarified that this is a strict requirement and a higher standard than merely stating someone manages the company's affairs or is involved in its day-to-day business.
application: The Court examined the specific averments in the complaint against the appellant.
It found that allegations like being "responsible for the day-to-day contact and business" were insufficient to meet the mandatory legal standard set by Section 141(1).
The Court reasoned that such general statements do not specifically establish that the appellant was both "in charge of" and "responsible to the company for the conduct of the business."
It concluded that the complaint failed to make the necessary and specific allegations to attract vicarious liability for the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the complaint was liable to be quashed because it was devoid of the mandatory averments required under Section 141(1) of the NI Act. The allegations made were too general and did not meet the high threshold needed to fasten vicarious criminal liability upon the appellant. Therefore, the Court allowed the appeal and quashed the criminal proceedings against him.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the complaint is liable to be quashed for being devoid of the mandatory averments required under Section 141(1) of the NI Act to fasten vicarious liability on the appellant.
appellant_arguments: The complaint lacks the mandatory averments required under Section 141(1) of the NI Act to hold the appellant vicariously liable.
The complaint fails to specify or elaborate on the appellant's role in the day-to-day affairs of the partnership firm.
The appellant cited the decisions in 'Anita Malhotra v. Apparel Export Promotion Council & Anr.' and 'Ashok Shewakramani & Ors. v. State of Andhra Pradesh & Anr.' to support the argument.
respondent_arguments: The averments in paragraphs 3 and 4 of the complaint are sufficient to satisfy the mandatory requirements of Section 141 of the NI Act.
The respondent relied on the decision in 'S.P. Mani and Mohan Dairy v. Dr. Snehalatha Elangovan' to support this contention.

cases.case_name: S.P. Mani and Mohan Dairy v. Dr. Snehalatha Elangovan
cases.principle: It was relied on for its holding that the principles of law concerning vicarious liability under Section 141 of the NI Act, as laid down in the Gunmala Sales Private Limited case, still hold the field and reflect the correct position of law.

cases.case_name: Gunmala Sales Private Limited v. Anu Mehta
cases.principle: It was relied on for its exhaustive review and summary of the legal requirements to establish vicarious liability against a director or partner under Section 141 of the NI Act.

cases.case_name: Ashok Shewakramani & Ors. v. State of Andhra Pradesh & Anr.
cases.principle: It was relied on for the specific legal interpretation that the phrases “was in charge of” and “was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company” in Section 141(1) of the NI Act must be read conjunctively, not disjunctively.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The statutory phrases “was in charge of” and “was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company” must be read conjunctively, not disjunctively.
obiter: The principles of law laid down in Gunmala Sales Private Limited still hold the field and reflect the correct position of law.
In the case on hand, we find clear and specific averments not only in the complaint but also in the statutory notice issued to the respondent.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The averments in the complaint are not sufficient to satisfy the mandatory requirements of Section 141(1) of the NI Act because the complaint fails to aver that the appellant was 'in charge of the conduct of the business of the company' at the relevant time. Merely stating that the partners are 'responsible for the day-to-day conduct and business of the company' is insufficient, as the statutory requirements must be read conjunctively.
legal_tests_applied: For the purpose of fastening vicarious liability under Section 141(1) of the NI Act, the words 'was in charge of' and 'was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company' cannot be read disjunctively and must be read conjunctively.
A complaint must contain clear and specific averments about the role of the accused, and an overall reading must disclose their specific involvement to justify proceeding against them.
why_appellant_lost: The respondent's complaint was found to be legally deficient as it only stated that the appellant, along with other partners, was 'responsible for the day-to-day conduct and business of the company' but crucially omitted the mandatory averment that the appellant was also 'in charge of the conduct of the business of the company' when the offence was committed.
The respondent misread the precedent in 'S.P. Mani and Mohan Dairy v. Dr. Snehalatha Elangovan', which clarifies that both statutory conditions for vicarious liability must be pleaded together.

An overall reading of the complaint failed to disclose any clear and specific role for the appellant; instead, it specifically implicated other accused (Nos. 2 and 3) in the acts of purchasing goods and issuing the cheque, thereby weakening the case against the appellant.
why_respondent_won: The appellant successfully demonstrated that the complaint lacked the specific, mandatory averments required by Section 141(1) of the NI Act to establish vicarious liability.

The appellant's argument was validated by the court's application of the principle from 'S.P. Mani’s case', which requires a conjunctive reading of the phrases 'was in charge of' and 'was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business'.

The appellant highlighted that the complaint, by specifically naming other accused for the substantive actions, failed to establish a prima facie case that the appellant was involved in the commission of the offence.
